answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From a letter Marie Curie wrote to her brother on March 18th, 1894, while she was a student in Paris. It is printed in Eve Curie’s biography Madame Curie, in Vincent Sheean’s English translation, and the wording is confirmed against the full text of that book.

source.heading: The letter

docMeta.dd: Madame Curie: A Biography, by Eve Curie
Letter from Marie to her brother, March 18th, 1894

source.excerpt: … It is difficult for me to tell you about my life in detail; it is so monotonous and, in fact, so uninteresting. Nevertheless I have no feeling of uniformity and I regret only one thing, which is that the days are so short and that they pass so quickly. One never notices what has been done; one can only see what remains to be done, and if one didn’t like the work it would be very discouraging.
trail: Eve Curie, Madame Curie, trans. Vincent Sheean (Heinemann, 1938) ↗: the letter headed “Marie to her brother, March 18th, 1894” contains the exact sentence, pp. 113–114.
Internet Archive catalog record ↗ for the first US edition: Madame Curie: A Biography, Eve Curie, translated by Vincent Sheean (Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Doran, 1937).
Wikiquote ↗ puts the line first in its sourced Quotes section, credited to a “Letter to her brother (1894)”.
source.cutTag: The popular quote stops at “remains to be done”
source.excerptNote: The quote that circulates is the first half of one sentence. In the letter, Curie goes on: “and if one didn’t like the work it would be very discouraging.”

author.name: Marie Curie
author.heading: About Marie Curie
author.bio: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, Marie Curie studied in Paris and went on to pioneer research on radioactivity. With Pierre Curie she discovered polonium and radium. She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.

misattribution.heading: How the line gets bent
misattribution.intro: This is one of the few popular Marie Curie lines that is genuine. Still, it gets cut short, and one reworded version is credited to someone else entirely.

items.why: A first-person rewording, “I never see what has been done; I only see what remains to be done,” appears in lists of Buddha quotes ↗ with no scripture or text cited. The wording matches Curie’s 1894 letter almost word for word.
The popular quote ends at “remains to be done.” In the printed letter ↗, the same sentence continues: “and if one didn’t like the work it would be very discouraging.”

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Marie Curie’s, from her letter to her brother of March 18th, 1894, as printed in Vincent Sheean’s translation of Eve Curie’s Madame Curie ↗.

context.heading: A student’s letter home
lead: In March 1894, Marie Skłodowska was a student in Paris. According to her daughter Eve’s biography, she had passed first in the master’s examination in physics in 1893 and would place second in mathematics in 1894. Writing to her brother, she called her life “so monotonous and, in fact, so uninteresting,” yet her only regret was “that the days are so short and that they pass so quickly.”

The line about never noticing what has been done comes in the middle of that letter. Further on she urges her brother to finish his doctor’s thesis: “We must have perseverance and above all confidence in ourselves.”
